AI has been worming its way into our everyday lives for years now, although it feels like an absolute age. If I had a nickel for everytime I heard a tech bro tell us that AI is inevitable so we should all get on board, I'd have enough money to buy back all the RAM they've taken from me. So with this in mind it's hardly surprising that yet another former game exec has come out with this exact line once again. Ex-Take Two boss Ben Feder, who oversaw games like Red Dead Redemption and Grand Theft Auto 4, has discussed with The Game Business how one day people will accept AI—it's just a matter of time. "When animation went from hand-drawn to computer animation, there was a massive wall of resistance," he says. "People didn’t think it looked good. Then Pixar launched Toy Story. They created a movie that not only was awesome, but used computer-generated animation and chose a subject matter that made the most of it, and did an amazing job with it. "Once Toy Story launched, all the resistance went away. My own view is that we are one Toy Story moment away from consumer acceptance of AI in videogames in the West. In the East, they’ve already accepted it." Feder is correct that the use of AI in game development does seem more widely accepted in countries like China and South Korea, where it's often viewed as an unremarkable part of the process. Still, for me the idea of comparing a beloved childhood film that was lovingly and painstakingly crafted with 10s of thousands of hand drawn story boards, clay models for characters, and multiple production teams, to a tool that cannot run without stolen ideas is mind-boggling. I have some faith that machine learning can be used to help people make their jobs easier—that is, if AI companies want to make a product that's actually helpful and not one just that will make loads of money before it all comes crumbling down. titre: Former GTA 4 and Red Dead boss thinks "we are one Toy Story moment away" from people accepting gen-AI in game development in the West
chapo: Ben Feder, the former Take-Two CEO who oversaw the launch of massive hits like Grand Theft Auto 4, Red Dead Redemption, Borderlands, and BioShock during his tenure, believes the resistance against gen-AI in games will vanish once the games industry has its 'Toy Story moment'. Read more
extrait: Ben Feder, the former Take-Two CEO who oversaw the launch of massive hits like Grand Theft Auto 4, Red Dead Redemption, Borderlands, and BioShock during his tenure, believes the resistance against gen-AI in games will vanish once the games industry has its 'Toy Story moment'. "When animation went from hand-drawn to computer animation, there was a massive wall of resistance," Feder told The Game Business. "People didn't think it looked good. Then Pixar launched Toy Story. They created a movie that not only was awesome, but used computer-generated animation and chose a subject matter that made the most of it, and did an amazing job with it." Feder argued that the success of Toy Story ended the resistance against computer-generated animation, and the same could happen to games. Feder added, "My own view is that we are one Toy Story moment away from consumer acceptance of AI in video games in the West. In the East, they've already accepted it." Feder, who currently heads up venture capital fund Tirta Ventures, is investing in AI-first games. He, however, doesn't necessarily believe AI will reduce development costs, but that it also offers other advantages that could help game makers keep up with shifting consumer tastes. "A lot of incumbents think about AI as a way of reducing costs, which it is," Feder said. "I query whether it will actually reduce costs, or will it just make games bigger for the same cost? But we're more interested in what AI can do to radically change gameplay." Feder views gen-AI simply as new technology that allows developers to do things they couldn't before. He likened it to Unreal Engine's instancing technology, which allowed Fortnite and other battle royale games to support 100+ players in a single server. "That's question number one as we think about what we invest in: Was this possible before AI?" Feder said of his VC firm's strategy. "And when AI gets better, does the game get better? That's harder for an incumbent to focus on, because they deploy a lot of capital, have enormous advantages in terms of distribution, capital, and IP, and all of that needs to be protected." There's been enormous pushback from players, developers and pundits against the use of gen-AI in games. Even so, more and more studios have revealed using some gen-AI during development, such as to assist with coding.
